subject: math
title: Grade 7 Exchange Rates and Interest: Converting Currencies, Simple Interest and Budgets
seo_title: Grade 7 Exchange Rates and Simple Interest Worksheets (Free, Answer Key) | Ontario Math
standard_text: Identify and compare exchange rates, and convert foreign currencies to Canadian dollars and vice versa
meta_desc: Free Grade 7 math worksheets on exchange rates and interest for the Ontario curriculum: convert Canadian dollars to US dollars, euros and yen and back, compare prices in two currencies, simple interest on savings and loans, and budgets for longer-term goals. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Foreign money to C$: multiply by the rate. C$ to foreign money: divide.
key_sub: With US$1 = C$1.35, US$40 × 1.35 = C$54 and C$270 ÷ 1.35 = US$200. Simple interest is I = Prt, with the rate as a decimal (3% = 0.03) and the time in years.
body_html:
Exchange rates

An exchange rate tells you how much one currency is worth in another. C$ means Canadian dollars, US$ means US dollars, € means euros and ¥ means Japanese yen. Real rates change every day, so this page uses sample rates, such as US$1 = C$1.35.

Read the rate as “1 foreign unit = some Canadian dollars”. Then:

You haveYou wantDo this (US$1 = C$1.35)
Foreign moneyCanadian dollarsMultiply by the rate: US$40 × 1.35 = C$54
Canadian dollarsForeign moneyDivide by the rate: C$270 ÷ 1.35 = US$200

Check your answer. One US dollar is worth more than one Canadian dollar here, so the C$ number must be the bigger one.

Example

Suppose €1 = C$1.50. How many euros do you get for C$300?

Each euro costs C$1.50. C$300 ÷ 1.50 = 200. Check: 200 × 1.50 = 300.

Answer: €200

Example

Suppose C$1 = ¥110. How many yen do you get for C$50?

This rate tells you what C$1 buys, so multiply: 50 × 110 = 5500.

Answer: ¥5500

Comparing prices

To compare prices in two currencies, change one price into the other currency first. Then compare.

Example

Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. A hoodie costs US$40 in the US and C$56 in Canada. Where is it cheaper?

US$40 × 1.35 = C$54. C$54 < C$56.

Answer: In the US, by C$2

Simple interest

Interest is the cost of using money. A bank pays you interest on savings. You pay interest when you borrow. Simple interest uses I = Prt: principal × yearly rate (as a decimal) × time in years.

Example

You save $800 at 3% simple interest per year for 2 years. How much interest do you earn?

3% = 0.03. I = $800 × 0.03 × 2 = $48. The balance is $800 + $48 = $848.

Answer: $48

Choosing an account, a loan or a card

Look at the whole cost, not just the rate: interest, monthly or annual fees and rewards. A low rate with a high fee can cost more. If you pay a credit card bill in full every month, the fee matters more than the rate. For a long-term goal, find what you still need and divide it by what you can save each month.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Multiplying when you should divide (C$270 × 1.35)C$ to US$ with US$1 = C$1.35: divide, C$270 ÷ 1.35 = US$200
Taking 35% off instead of dividing by 1.35Dividing by 1.35 is not the same as subtracting 35%
Comparing US$20 with C$25 directlyConvert to the same currency first
Using the rate as a whole number (3 for 3%)Write the rate as a decimal: 3% = 0.03
Using 6 for 6 monthsTime is in years: 6 months = 0.5
Giving the interest as the balanceBalance = principal + interest
Choosing the account with the higher rate onlySubtract the fees and compare what is left

faq.q: What do Grade 7 students learn in financial literacy in Ontario?
faq.a: Grade 7 students compare exchange rates and convert between Canadian dollars and other currencies, plan budgets for longer-term goals, and learn how interest rates affect saving and borrowing. They also compare bank accounts, loans and credit cards.

faq.q: How do you convert Canadian dollars to US dollars?
faq.a: If the rate is written as US$1 = C$1.35, divide the Canadian amount by 1.35: C$270 ÷ 1.35 = US$200. To go from US dollars to Canadian dollars, multiply by 1.35.

faq.q: How do you calculate simple interest in Grade 7?
faq.a: Use I = Prt: principal × yearly rate as a decimal × time in years. For $800 at 3% for 2 years, I = 800 × 0.03 × 2 = $48.

faq.q: Are the exchange rates on these worksheets real?
faq.a: No. Real exchange rates change every day, so every question gives a sample rate, such as US$1 = C$1.35. Students learn the method and can then use the rate posted by a bank on the day.

items.q: Suppose 1 US dollar is worth 1.35 Canadian dollars (US$1 = C$1.35). Which is worth more?
items.e: You need C$1.35 to buy one US dollar, so 1 US dollar is worth more than 1 Canadian dollar. An exchange rate tells you how much of one currency equals one unit of another.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. To change Canadian dollars into US dollars, what should you do?
items.e: Each US dollar costs C$1.35, so count how many groups of 1.35 fit into your Canadian dollars: divide by 1.35. You get fewer US dollars than Canadian dollars.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.25. How many US dollars do you get for C$100?
items.e: Each US dollar costs C$1.25, so divide: C$100.00 ÷ 1.25 = US$80.00. Check: US$80.00 × 1.25 = C$100.00. (US$125.00 multiplies instead of dividing.)

items.q: Suppose €1 = C$1.50. How many euros do you get for C$300?
items.e: Each euro costs C$1.50, so divide: C$300.00 ÷ 1.50 = €200.00. Check: €200.00 × 1.50 = C$300.00. (€450.00 multiplies instead of dividing.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.40. How many US dollars do you get for C$70?
items.e: Each US dollar costs C$1.40, so divide: C$70.00 ÷ 1.40 = US$50.00. Check: US$50.00 × 1.40 = C$70.00.

items.q: Suppose C$1 = ¥110 (Japanese yen). How many yen do you get for C$50?
items.e: Each Canadian dollar is worth 110 yen, so multiply: C$50.00 × 110 = ¥5500. (¥160 adds instead of multiplying.)

items.q: Suppose C$1 = 13 Mexican pesos. How many pesos do you get for C$40?
items.e: Each Canadian dollar is worth 13 pesos, so multiply: C$40.00 × 13 = 520 pesos.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. How many US dollars do you get for C$270?
items.e: Each US dollar costs C$1.35, so divide: C$270.00 ÷ 1.35 = US$200.00. Check: US$200.00 × 1.35 = C$270.00. (US$175.50 takes 35% off, but dividing by 1.35 is not the same as subtracting 35%.)

items.q: Suppose €1 = C$1.50. How many euros do you get for C$450?
Suppose C$1 = US$0.75. How many US dollars do you get for C$80?
items.e: Each Canadian dollar is worth 0.75 US dollars, so multiply: C$80.00 × 0.75 = US$60.00. This time the rate tells you what one Canadian dollar is worth, so you multiply. (US$106.67 divides instead.)

items.q: Suppose C$1 = €0.68. How many euros do you get for C$250?
items.e: Each Canadian dollar is worth 0.68 euros, so multiply: C$250.00 × 0.68 = €170.00.

items.q: Suppose C$1 = ¥110. How many yen do you get for C$125?
items.e: Each Canadian dollar is worth 110 yen, so multiply: C$125.00 × 110 = ¥13 750.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.36. How many US dollars do you get for C$340?
items.e: Each US dollar costs C$1.36, so divide: C$340.00 ÷ 1.36 = US$250.00. Check: US$250.00 × 1.36 = C$340.00.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.38. About how many US dollars do you get for C$700?
items.e: Round the rate: 1.38 ≈ 1.4. C$700 ÷ 1.4 = US$500, so about US$500. (About US$1000 multiplies by 1.4. You always get fewer US dollars than Canadian dollars at this rate.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. How many US dollars do you get for C$100? Round to the nearest cent.
items.e: Each US dollar costs C$1.35, so divide: C$100.00 ÷ 1.35 = 74.074… ≈ US$74.07. (US$65.00 takes off 35% instead of dividing.)

items.q: Suppose €1 = C$1.48. How many euros do you get for C$200? Round to the nearest cent.
Suppose US$1 = C$1.25. What is C$1 worth in US dollars?
items.e: Divide: C$1 ÷ 1.25 = US$0.80. Check: US$0.80 × 1.25 = C$1.00. (US$0.75 just takes 25¢ off; that is not the same as dividing by 1.25.)

items.q: Use the sample exchange rates. How many euros do you get for C$600?
items.e: The board shows €1 = C$1.50. C$600 ÷ 1.50 = €400.00. Check: 400 × C$1.50 = C$600. (€900.00 multiplies; €444.44 uses the US dollar rate.)

items.q: Use the sample exchange rates. How many yen do you get for C$90?
items.e: The board shows ¥100 = C$0.90. C$90 ÷ 0.90 = 100 groups of ¥100, and 100 × ¥100 = ¥10 000. (¥100 forgets that each group is ¥100, not ¥1.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.25. Owen changes C$500 into US dollars for a trip to New York. The bank first takes a C$5 fee from the C$500. How many US dollars does he get?
items.e: After the fee: C$500 − C$5 = C$495. Convert: C$495 ÷ 1.25 = US$396.00. (US$400.00 forgets the fee; US$395.00 takes the fee off in US dollars after converting.)

items.q: The double number line shows US$1 = C$1.35. What is US$4 in Canadian dollars?
items.e: Each US dollar is worth C$1.35, so multiply: US$4.00 × 1.35 = C$5.40.

items.q: Suppose €1 = C$1.50. To change euros into Canadian dollars, what should you do?
items.e: Each euro is worth C$1.50, so 2 euros are worth 2 × C$1.50. Multiply by 1.50. You get more Canadian dollars than euros.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. What is US$10 in Canadian dollars?
items.e: Each US dollar is worth C$1.35, so multiply: US$10.00 × 1.35 = C$13.50. (C$7.41 divides instead of multiplying.)

items.q: Suppose €1 = C$1.50. What is €40 in Canadian dollars?
items.e: Each euro is worth C$1.50, so multiply: €40.00 × 1.50 = C$60.00.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.30. What is US$25 in Canadian dollars?
items.e: Each US dollar is worth C$1.30, so multiply: US$25.00 × 1.30 = C$32.50.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. What is US$200 in Canadian dollars?
items.e: Each US dollar is worth C$1.35, so multiply: US$200.00 × 1.35 = C$270.00. (C$70.00 is only the extra 35¢ on each dollar.)

items.q: Suppose €1 = C$1.45. What is €80 in Canadian dollars?
items.e: Each euro is worth C$1.45, so multiply: €80.00 × 1.45 = C$116.00.

items.q: Suppose C$1 = ¥110. What is ¥5500 in Canadian dollars?
items.e: C$1 buys 110 yen, so divide: ¥5500 ÷ 110 = C$50.00. Check: 50.00 × 110 = ¥5500. (Multiplying would give a huge number of dollars, which cannot be right.)

items.q: Suppose C$1 = 13 Mexican pesos. What is 780 pesos in Canadian dollars?
items.e: C$1 buys 13 pesos, so divide: 780 pesos ÷ 13 = C$60.00. Check: 60.00 × 13 = 780 pesos.

items.q: Suppose C$1 = US$0.75. What is US$45 in Canadian dollars?
items.e: C$1 buys 0.75 US dollars, so divide: US$45.00 ÷ 0.75 = C$60.00. Check: 60.00 × 0.75 = US$45.00. (C$33.75 multiplies, but the rate tells you what C$1 is worth, so divide.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.40. A pair of jeans costs US$35.50. What is that in Canadian dollars?
items.e: Each US dollar is worth C$1.40, so multiply: US$35.50 × 1.40 = C$49.70.

items.q: Use the sample exchange rates. A hotel room in Paris costs €120 a night. What is that in Canadian dollars?
items.e: Each euro is worth C$1.50, so multiply: €120.00 × 1.50 = C$180.00.

items.q: Use the sample exchange rates. A train ticket in Japan costs ¥5000. What is that in Canadian dollars?
items.e: The board shows ¥100 = C$0.90. ¥5000 is 50 groups of ¥100. 50 × C$0.90 = C$45.00. (C$4500.00 multiplies 5000 × 0.90 and forgets that the rate is for ¥100.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.37. A T-shirt costs US$19.99. What is that in Canadian dollars? Round to the nearest cent.
items.e: Each US dollar is worth C$1.37, so multiply: US$19.99 × 1.37 = 27.3863 ≈ C$27.39. (C$14.59 divides instead of multiplying.)

items.q: Suppose €1 = C$1.48. What is €250 in Canadian dollars?
items.e: Each euro is worth C$1.48, so multiply: €250.00 × 1.48 = C$370.00.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.38. About how much is US$49.95 in Canadian dollars?
items.e: Round: US$49.95 ≈ US$50 and 1.38 ≈ 1.4. 50 × 1.4 = 70, so about C$70. (About C$35 divides; about C$50 forgets to convert.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. Nathan says US$80 is about C$59. Is he right?
items.e: US dollars are worth more than Canadian dollars at this rate, so the C$ amount must be more than 80. 80 × 1.35 = 108, so US$80 is about C$108. Nathan divided instead of multiplying.

items.q: A bank sells US$300 for C$405. What exchange rate did it use?
items.e: Find the cost of US$1: C$405 ÷ 300 = 1.35, so US$1 = C$1.35. (0.74 divides the other way; 105 is C$405 − 300.)

items.q: Suppose €1 = C$1.50. On a trip to Paris, Mateo buys a souvenir for €15 and a T-shirt for €25. What is the total in Canadian dollars?
items.e: Total in euros: €15 + €25 = €40. Convert: 40 × 1.50 = C$60.00. (C$26.67 divides; C$40.00 forgets to convert.)

items.q: A bank sells US dollars at US$1 = C$1.35 and buys them back at US$1 = C$1.30. After a trip, Ava sells US$100 back to the bank. How many Canadian dollars does she get?
items.e: When you sell US dollars back, the bank uses its buying rate: 100 × 1.30 = C$130.00. (C$135.00 uses the selling rate. The difference between the two rates is how the bank earns money.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. A book costs US$20 in the US and C$25 in Canada. Where is it cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Convert to the same currency: US$20.00 × 1.35 = C$27.00. Compare with C$25.00. Canada is cheaper, by C$27.00 − C$25.00 = C$2.00. (Comparing 20 with 25 directly mixes two currencies.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. A hoodie costs US$40 in the US and C$56 in Canada. Where is it cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Convert to the same currency: US$40.00 × 1.35 = C$54.00. Compare with C$56.00. The US is cheaper, by C$56.00 − C$54.00 = C$2.00.

items.q: Suppose €1 = C$1.50. Sneakers cost €80 in Paris and C$115 in Toronto. Where are they cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Convert to the same currency: €80.00 × 1.50 = C$120.00. Compare with C$115.00. Toronto is cheaper, by C$120.00 − C$115.00 = C$5.00.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.25. A video game costs US$60 in the US and C$75 in Canada. Where is it cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Convert to the same currency: US$60.00 × 1.25 = C$75.00. Compare with C$75.00. They cost the same. Different numbers can still be the same price in different currencies.

items.q: Suppose C$1 = ¥110. Headphones cost ¥8800 in Tokyo and C$85 in Vancouver. Where are they cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Convert to the same currency: ¥8800 ÷ 110 = C$80.00. Compare with C$85.00. Tokyo is cheaper, by C$85.00 − C$80.00 = C$5.00. (Here you divide, because the rate tells you what C$1 buys.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.40. A bottle of maple syrup costs US$15 in a US store and C$20 in Canada. Where is it cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Convert to the same currency: US$15.00 × 1.40 = C$21.00. Compare with C$20.00. Canada is cheaper, by C$21.00 − C$20.00 = C$1.00.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. A pair of earbuds costs US$24 online in the US and C$32.40 in Canada. Where are they cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Convert to the same currency: US$24.00 × 1.35 = C$32.40. Compare with C$32.40. They cost the same.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. A 1 kg bag of coffee costs US$12 in the US and C$17 in Canada. Where is it cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Convert to the same currency: US$12.00 × 1.35 = C$16.20. Compare with C$17.00. The US is cheaper, by C$17.00 − C$16.20 = C$0.80.

items.q: Use the sample exchange rates. The same jacket costs C$150 in Canada, US$115 in the US and €95 in France. Where is it cheapest?
items.e: Convert both to C$: US$115 × 1.35 = C$155.25; €95 × 1.50 = C$142.50. €95 in France is the cheapest. (The smallest number is not always the lowest price.)

items.q: Which sample exchange rate gives you the most US dollars for C$100?
items.e: You divide by the rate, so the smallest rate gives the most US dollars. C$100 ÷ 1.32 ≈ US$75.76, but C$100 ÷ 1.40 ≈ US$71.43. US$1 = C$1.32 is best.

items.q: The sample exchange rate changes from US$1 = C$1.25 to US$1 = C$1.40. What happens to the cost of a US$50 hotel night in Canadian dollars?
c: It falls from C$70 to C$62.50
It rises from C$62.50 to C$70
items.e: Before: 50 × 1.25 = C$62.50. After: 50 × 1.40 = C$70.00. Each US dollar now costs more, so the room costs more in Canadian dollars. (C$0.15 is the change for just US$1.)

items.q: Amira’s family needs €200 for a trip. Suppose €1 = C$1.40 in May and €1 = C$1.50 in June. How much more does the €200 cost in June than in May?
items.e: May: 200 × 1.40 = C$280. June: 200 × 1.50 = C$300. Difference: C$300 − C$280 = C$20.00. (C$0.10 is the change in the rate for only €1.)

items.q: Suppose €1 = C$1.45. A soccer jersey costs €70 in Spain and C$100 in Canada. Where is it cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Convert to the same currency: €70.00 × 1.45 = C$101.50. Compare with C$100.00. Canada is cheaper, by C$101.50 − C$100.00 = C$1.50.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.30. A laptop costs US$800 in the US and C$1000 in Canada. Where is it cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Convert to the same currency: US$800.00 × 1.30 = C$1040.00. Compare with C$1000.00. Canada is cheaper, by C$1040.00 − C$1000.00 = C$40.00.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. A US website sells a game for US$30 plus US$10 shipping. A Canadian store sells it for C$50. Which is cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: US total: US$30 + US$10 = US$40. 40 × 1.35 = C$54. Canada is cheaper, by C$54 − C$50 = C$4.00. (The US, by C$9.50 forgets the shipping: 30 × 1.35 = C$40.50.)

items.q: Suppose €1 = C$1.50 and US$1 = C$1.35. Which is worth more: €10 or US$11?
items.e: Change both to C$: €10 × 1.50 = C$15.00; US$11 × 1.35 = C$14.85. €10 is worth C$0.15 more. (US$11 looks bigger only because 11 > 10.)

items.q: Suppose C$1 = ¥110. A bowl of ramen costs ¥1100 in Tokyo and C$14 in Vancouver. Where is it cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Convert to the same currency: ¥1100 ÷ 110 = C$10.00. Compare with C$14.00. Tokyo is cheaper, by C$14.00 − C$10.00 = C$4.00.

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. Mei finds skates for US$90 on a US website, plus C$15 shipping to Canada. A store in Winnipeg sells them for C$135. Which is cheaper, and by how much?
items.e: Website: 90 × 1.35 = C$121.50, plus C$15 = C$136.50. Winnipeg is cheaper, by C$1.50. (The website, by C$13.50 forgets the shipping.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.25. A bike costs US$400 in the US and C$600 in Canada. The Canadian price is what percent more than the US price?
items.e: US price in C$: 400 × 1.25 = C$500. Difference: C$600 − C$500 = C$100. 100 ÷ 500 = 0.2 = 20%. (50% compares 600 with 400 without converting; 17% divides by 600 instead of the US price.)

items.q: Why can you not compare US$20 and C$25 just by looking at the numbers?
c: Prices in the US include tax
The units are worth different amounts
items.e: A US dollar and a Canadian dollar are worth different amounts, like comparing metres and centimetres. Convert both prices into the same currency first.

sets.title: Simple interest on savings and loans

items.q: What is interest?
c: The tax added to a price
Money paid for using someone else’s money
A fee for opening a bank account
items.e: When you save, the bank uses your money and pays you interest. When you borrow, you pay interest for using the lender’s money.

items.q: In the simple interest formula I = Prt, what does r stand for?
c: The yearly interest rate, as a decimal
items.e: I is the interest, P is the principal (the money at the start), r is the yearly rate written as a decimal (3% = 0.03), and t is the time in years.

items.q: To use a 3% interest rate in I = Prt, what number do you use for r?
items.e: Percent means out of 100: 3% = 3 ÷ 100 = 0.03. Using 3 would make the interest 100 times too big.

items.q: What is the simple interest on $500 at 2% per year for 1 year?
What is the simple interest on $800 at 3% per year for 2 years?
Aiden saves $1200 in an account that pays 2.5% simple interest per year. How much is in the account after 1 year?
Noah borrows $600 at 8% simple interest per year. How much must he pay back after 1 year?
items.e: I = Prt = $600.00 × 0.08 × 1 = $48.00. Total: $600.00 + $48.00 = $648.00. When you borrow, you pay back the loan plus the interest.

items.q: What is the simple interest on a $1500 loan at 6% per year for 2 years?
What is the simple interest on $2000 at 4% per year for 6 months?
items.e: I = Prt = $2000.00 × 0.04 × 0.5 = $40.00. 6 months is half a year, so t = 0.5. ($480.00 uses t = 6; $80.00 is a full year.)

items.q: $400 earns $12 of simple interest in 1 year. What is the yearly interest rate?
items.e: r = I ÷ (P × t) = 12 ÷ 400 = 0.03 = 3%. (12% uses the dollars as the percent; 33% divides 400 by 12.)

items.q: $900 earns 2% simple interest per year. How many years will it take to earn $54 of interest?
items.e: Interest each year: $900 × 0.02 = $18. $54 ÷ $18 = 3 years. (27 divides $54 by 2; 18 is the interest for one year, not the time.)

items.q: Which earns more simple interest in 3 years: $1000 at 2% per year, or $1500 at 1% per year?
items.e: $1000 × 0.02 × 3 = $60. $1500 × 0.01 × 3 = $45. $1000 at 2% earns $15 more. A higher rate can beat a bigger principal.

items.q: $500 is saved for a few years. Which earns more simple interest: 3% for 2 years, or 2% for 3 years?
items.e: 3% for 2 years: $500 × 0.03 × 2 = $30. 2% for 3 years: $500 × 0.02 × 3 = $30. They earn the same, because 0.03 × 2 = 0.02 × 3.

items.q: How does a higher interest rate affect savers and borrowers?
c: Savings grow slower; loans cost less
Savings grow faster; loans cost more
items.e: A higher rate means more interest. For a saver, the bank pays more, so savings grow faster. For a borrower, a loan costs more to pay back.

items.q: A bank pays 2% interest on savings and charges 7% interest on loans. Why are the rates different?
c: The bank earns money from the gap
Savers pay the bank to save
Loans are always paid back early
items.e: The bank lends out money that people save. It pays savers 2% and charges borrowers 7%, so it earns money from the difference.

items.q: Kai’s credit card charges 19.99% interest per year. He leaves a $500 balance unpaid for 1 year. Using simple interest, how much interest is that?
items.e: 19.99% = 0.1999. I = $500 × 0.1999 × 1 = $99.95, almost $100. (Real cards add interest even faster, so paying the full bill on time is the best plan.)

items.q: A family borrows $3000 at 5% simple interest per year for 4 years. How much do they pay back in total?
Chloe borrows $1200 for a laptop at 5% simple interest for 1 year. She pays it back in 12 equal monthly payments. How much is each payment?
$700 at 3% simple interest earns $21 each year. How much interest does it earn in 4 years?
items.e: Simple interest is the same every year. 4 × $21 = $84.00. ($784.00 is the balance, not the interest; $25.00 adds 4 instead of multiplying.)

items.q: How much must you save at 4% simple interest per year to earn $60 in 1 year?
Which is a long-term financial goal for a Grade 7 student?
items.e: A long-term goal takes many months or years of saving. Saving for college or university is long-term; the others are short-term spending.

items.q: Maya wants C$1200 for a school trip in 10 months. She already has C$300 saved. How much must she save each month?
items.e: Still needed: C$1200 − C$300 = C$900. Each month: C$900 ÷ 10 = C$90.00. (C$120.00 forgets the C$300 already saved.)

items.q: Sofia’s budget is balanced. How much does she save each month?
items.e: Money in: $240 + $80 = $320. Spending: $45 + $60 + $55 = $160. Savings: $320 − $160 = $160.00. ($320.00 is all the money in; $80.00 forgets the allowance.)

items.q: Sofia wants a $960 bike. Using this budget, how many months will it take to save for it?
items.e: She saves $320 − $160 = $160 each month. $960 ÷ $160 = 6 months. (3 months divides by all the money in, $320; 4 months divides by the job pay only.)

items.q: You keep $1000 in a savings account for 1 year. Which account leaves you with more money?
items.e: Account A: interest $1000 × 0.025 = $25, fees 12 × $3 = $36, so you lose $11. Account B: interest $1000 × 0.01 = $10, no fees. $10 − (−$11) = $21, so Account B, by $21. (Account A, by $15 forgets the monthly fees.)

items.q: You keep $5000 in a savings account for 1 year. Which account leaves you with more money?
items.e: Account A: $5000 × 0.025 = $125 interest, minus $36 in fees = $89. Account B: $5000 × 0.01 = $50. $89 − $50 = $39, so Account A, by $39. With more money saved, the higher rate beats the fee. (Account A, by $75 forgets the fees.)

items.q: Suppose you carry a $1000 balance on a credit card for a whole year. Using simple interest, which card costs less?
Jayden always pays his credit card bill in full by the due date, so he never pays interest. Which card is better for him?
c: Card B, because its rate is lower
Card A, because it has no fee
Card B, because it has a fee
items.e: If the bill is always paid in full, no interest is charged, so the rate does not matter. Card A has no annual fee, so it costs Jayden $0. Card B costs $40 a year.

items.q: A family borrows $2000 for a canoe. Loan A is 6% simple interest for 2 years. Loan B is 5% simple interest for 3 years. Which loan costs less interest?
items.e: Loan A: $2000 × 0.06 × 2 = $240. Loan B: $2000 × 0.05 × 3 = $300. Loan A costs $60 less. A lower rate does not always mean less interest; the time matters too.

items.q: A phone costs $600. Hana can save $50 a month for 12 months and then buy it, or borrow $600 now at 10% simple interest and pay it back in 1 year. How much more does borrowing cost?
items.e: Interest on the loan: $600 × 0.10 × 1 = $60. Saving first costs exactly $600. Borrowing gets the phone sooner but costs $60 more. ($6000 uses 10 instead of 0.10.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.35. Emma wants US$400 of spending money for a trip to Florida. She has C$300 saved and saves C$40 a week. How many more weeks until she has enough?
items.e: US$400 × 1.35 = C$540. Still needed: C$540 − C$300 = C$240. C$240 ÷ C$40 = 6 weeks. (3 weeks forgets to convert the US dollars; 14 weeks forgets the C$300 already saved.)

items.q: Liam puts $2000 in a savings account at 3% simple interest per year. After 2 years, will he have enough for a $2100 trip?
items.e: Interest: $2000 × 0.03 × 2 = $120. Balance: $2120. $2120 − $2100 = $20, so yes, with $20 to spare. (No, $40 short uses only 1 year of interest.)

items.q: Lucas’s family is going to France next summer. Lucas wants €300 of spending money. Suppose €1 = C$1.50. He saves the C$ amount over 9 months. How much is that each month?
items.e: €300 × 1.50 = C$450. C$450 ÷ 9 = C$50.00 a month. (C$33.33 forgets to convert the euros; C$22.22 divides by 1.50.)

items.q: A credit card gives 1% cash back. Zoe’s family spends $2400 on the card in a year and pays the bill in full each month. How much cash back do they get?
Priya has $1500 from summer jobs. It could sit in a drawer, or go in a savings account at 2% simple interest per year. How much more will she have after 3 years with the account?
items.e: Interest: $1500 × 0.02 × 3 = $90.00. Money in a drawer earns nothing. ($30.00 is only 1 year; $1590.00 is the whole balance.)

items.q: Arjun keeps $800 in an account that pays 1.5% simple interest per year but charges a $2 fee each month. How much is in the account after 1 year?
Benjamin earns $300 a month and saves 20% of it. How many months will it take to save $900?
items.e: 20% of $300: $300 × 0.20 = $60 a month. $900 ÷ $60 = 15 months. (3 months saves all $300 each month; 45 uses $20 instead of 20%.)

items.q: A store offers to let a family pay for a $400 bike over 1 year at 15% simple interest. A grandparent offers to lend the $400 with no interest. How much does the family save by borrowing from the grandparent?
items.e: Store interest: $400 × 0.15 × 1 = $60. The grandparent charges $0, so they save $60.00. ($460.00 is the total paid to the store; $6000.00 uses 15 instead of 0.15.)

items.q: Suppose US$1 = C$1.36. A summer hockey camp in Michigan costs US$350. Ethan’s family pays the C$ amount in 4 equal monthly payments. How much is each payment?
items.e: US$350 × 1.36 = C$476. C$476 ÷ 4 = C$119.00. (C$87.50 forgets to convert; C$64.34 divides instead of multiplying.)

items.q: Leah borrows $900 for a bike at 6% simple interest for 1 year and pays it back in 12 equal monthly payments. How much is each payment?
items.e: Interest: $900 × 0.06 = $54. Total: $954. Each month: $954 ÷ 12 = $79.50. ($75.00 forgets the interest.)
